article.title: Chicago DSA Should Invest in Childcare as an Organizing Skill
article.author: Midwestern Socialist -- Chicago DSA
article.content: Caregivers looking after children of any age, but especially young ones, must offer proper nourishment and hydration, mental clarity, flexibility, a sense of joy, a sense of safety, and the ability to communicate clearly. Many of the skills that childcare requires overlap with the skills that make good organizers. If we, as socialists and as a growing political organization in the city of Chicago, want to expand our reach, we need to grow our childcare operation. If we want to fight for a better future for our children, and that includes the children of our members, we have to build structures to take care of them now. As our organization develops, acquires new office space in different areas of the city, expands meetings, and onboards new members, integrating our membership into our Child Watch program should be key to new member’s introduction to the chapter. I’ve been doing Child Watch at General Chapter Meetings and Endorsement forums for the past year. At my first general meeting, a little overwhelmed and distracted by all the new terms and processes, I heard the noises of kids coming from another room. As a doula and former nanny, I immediately wished I could just be in that room with the kids instead of trying to figure out how I should vote. Soon I found myself in the childcare room, but also increasingly motivated to balance my participation in our highest chapter decision-making body with my responsibility to our member’s children. As it stands, there is a small pool of Child Watch volunteers who work with the GCM subcommittee to make this care happen for every meeting. We hang out with the kids, chase after the toddlers, do arts and crafts, and talk with the older children. We bring them in at the end to sing Solidarity Forever (if they don’t need to go home for naptime before the meeting is over). When there’s a vote or debate on something one of our volunteers really values, we cover for each other to be able to go in and support what we care about. Oftentimes, we all discuss the resolutions together and then vote on Zoom from the child room. Child Watch gives members an opportunity to participate in our large meetings, meet people they might not organize with otherwise, and connect with the parents of our socialist future. It should not be dependent on a small group of organizers, who are, of course, mostly women and parents, to put on for every meeting. It is a valuable skill to be able to be present with children, and it strengthens our organization to allow parents to be present as members while still prioritizing the needs of their children through communication with the Child Watch volunteers. How can we grow this program For members without formal experience with children, the Child Watch program can produce a guide and opportunities for training to get people prepared to help. Specifically, we may choose to require CPR training and a basic conversation for first-time volunteers about child safety, as well as “do’s” and “dont’s” of working with children, group management of multiple ages, and parent communication. Many of our members are educators, and most understandably want a break from the day job when they come to meetings. However, since the skill set exists already within our chapter, it is our job to tap into it and to convince our membership that it is an advantage and a gift to care for each other as we make decisions and prioritize in-person, democratic processes. A little effort goes a long way. We have so much to learn from each other, and our General Chapter Meetings are a great place to meet comrades organizing in other parts of the city and doing different types of committee work. Child Watch is a great place for this to happen, and can become a hub for our members connecting across disciplines within our chapter. Once members train and participate in Child Watch at a General Chapter Meeting, they should be empowered to take those skills back to their committees and events, and encouraged to plan and execute Child Watch at larger in-person meetings on a case-by-case basis. In order to create these spaces for debate and ensure that all members can be included in the conversation, we need to prioritize the skill of childcare so that parents curious about our work and just getting into socialist organizing will feel welcomed and comfortable coming as they are. Participating in Child Watch is also a low barrier to entry for new members to learn how our chapter functions, giving them concrete tasks to do that can help them to plug into how our chapter functions. I am a firm believer that lifting the curtain on how our chapter works can empower our members to help make it happen, spread the load and make the lift of organizing our membership easier.
